answer.rationale: The tempting move is memory_c2 (switching primary supply to the low-cost vendor cut unit cost sharply, clean onboarding) because the quote alone satisfies the 18% mandate. But the mandate is only half the objective: TCO must fall WITHOUT increasing delivery risk, and the line is at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer and 14 days to expiry. A primary-vendor migration under those conditions concentrates all execution risk in the exact window where there is no slack to absorb a slipped first shipment; memory_c2's 'quick onboarding' was recorded under conditions we cannot confirm resembled a 94%-utilization, 14-day cutover, which is why I am spending verification on it rather than acting on it. memory_c1 and memory_c6 point the other way (incumbent continuity across two cycles, no migration work; multi-year terms unlock volume pricing without narrowing scope), and memory_c4 is the highest-leverage fit: benchmarking against market rates moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms. The low-cost quote is therefore most valuable as leverage, not as an immediate switch \u2014 it lets me pursue most of the 18% with no migration exposure. I want the c4 source record to check whether the recovered margin was material enough to plausibly close an 18% gap or merely a few points, since that determines whether negotiation is sufficient or only partial. add_second_source (memory_c3) is the right structural answer to single-point-of-failure but it adds cost rather than cutting it and does not resolve a contract that expires in 14 days; it is the natural next-cycle decision. defer_decision (memory_c5) worked for a non-critical, month-to-month service \u2014 this contract does not auto-renew, so deferring means unpriced exposure on the primary line, a materially different situation. I am scoping this as a guarded step: negotiate a short-horizon, benchmarked renewal that keeps scope intact and preserves the option to qualify the low-cost vendor as a second source next cycle, rather than locking a long multi-year term on price alone. Downstream value risk: an 18% cut pursued purely on unit price can be absorbed by the supplier as quieter degradation in quality, lead-time reliability, or invoicing accuracy \u2014 costs that reappear as scrap and line stoppage rather than in the price line \u2014 so any negotiated terms must hold scope and delivery commitments explicit and measured, not just the headline number.
